key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the autopay-minimum option reduced minimum-only payments by 23% at six months but did not reduce credit card debt, and it lowered autopay enrollment while increasing missed payments.
methodology: Field experiment (nudge in autopay enrollment default) on real credit-card accounts, six-month follow-up.
why_it_matters: Shows a nudge can move an enrollment-like behavioral metric without moving the real financial outcome, and can create new harms — the exact 'vanity enrollment' risk the support team is warning about for round-up sign-ups.
limitations: Credit-card debt paydown context, not a savings product
no measure of amount saved or persistence beyond six months
relevance_reason: Directly tests whether a choice-architecture nudge that raises a headline behavioral metric also improves the substantive outcome, the crux of the brief's enrollment-vs-vanity trade-off.

key_finding: A state-of-the-art review summarizes how automatic enrollment and default investment options affect participation and contribution rates short- and long-term, including potential negative effects on participant engagement.
methodology: Narrative literature overview, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a recent synthesis of the persistence and engagement costs of auto-enrollment defaults that echo the support team's objection, useful as a checklist of long-run harms to watch for.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app
no effect sizes given in the abstract
employer-as-trusted-intermediary mechanism does not carry over
relevance_reason: Recent synthesis of default-effect literature covering persistence, framing, and engagement costs, useful background despite the employer-plan setting.

key_finding: Argues default enrollment raises short-term retirement participation but induces long-term passivity (low contribution rates, inactive account management, churn), so participation alone does not demonstrate welfare improvement.
methodology: Narrative policy article, abstract-only, no primary data reported.
why_it_matters: States plainly the support team's exact worry — that default-driven enrollment can be a vanity metric masking disengagement — though argued from the employer-pension literature without new data.
limitations: Employer retirement system, not a consumer app
narrative synthesis, zero citations
no effect sizes given
relevance_reason: Articulates the passive-enrollment-as-vanity-metric argument central to the brief's internal debate, though evidentiary weight is weak.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for downstream (later) effects of default choice architecture, identifying time course of choice, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators of whether default effects persist.
methodology: Theoretical review and research-agenda paper synthesizing prior consumer-behavior findings, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a general, consumer-behavior (not employer-plan) framework for predicting when a default's initial enrollment effect will or will not persist and who it will affect differently — useful for designing the 6-12 month measurement plan.
limitations: Conceptual/theoretical, no new effect sizes
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: A recent, consumer-focused theoretical synthesis of exactly the persistence and heterogeneity questions the brief asks about.

key_finding: Random assignment to Medicare Part D default plans shows large, persistent enrollment and drug-utilization effects, with beneficiary passivity remaining nearly insensitive even when the default causes substantial welfare losses.
methodology: Natural experiments and random assignment to default options among low-income Medicare beneficiaries.
why_it_matters: Provides rigorous causal evidence that default effects can persist strongly even against beneficiaries' own interests, sharpening the brief's distributional question about who is helped versus harmed by defaulting people in.
limitations: Health insurance/drug plan choice, not a liquid consumer savings product
low-income Medicare population differs from app users choosing round-up savings
relevance_reason: Rigorous, high-profile evidence on persistence and distributional harm of default enrollment in a non-financial-services domain, useful by analogy for the brief's welfare question.

key_finding: Across nine 401(k) plans, automatic enrollment raises steady-state savings by only 0.6% of income and default auto-escalation by 0.3%, because employees leave firms, withdraw balances, and opt out of escalation.
methodology: Analysis of administrative data from nine 401(k) plans incorporating turnover, withdrawal, and opt-out dynamics.
why_it_matters: The clearest statement of our support team's objection: the enrolment lift is real at signup and much smaller later once withdrawal and opt-out are accounted for.
limitations: Retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
abstract gives income-share effects rather than app-comparable enrolment/engagement rates
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving amounts, which the brief asked us to test against.

key_finding: Nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees into Germany's public pension raised participation by 23 percentage points, but most enrolled individuals subsequently actively opt out, with default effects stronger when incentives are high or enrollment status is unknown.
methodology: Natural experiment using administrative and survey data around Germany's public pension auto-enrollment rollout.
why_it_matters: Shows a large headline default effect on participation can coexist with substantial subsequent opt-out, directly bearing on whether opt-out enrollment produces durable or nominal sign-ups.
limitations: Public pension system with government as intermediary, not a self-directed consumer app
no data on savings amounts or engagement beyond opt-out status
relevance_reason: Recent, large-scale evidence quantifying both the size of a default effect and the rate of subsequent active opt-out, informing the persistence question.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months across over 100 US plans and a UK panel, are substantially attenuated by 36 months, though inequality reduction persists; a life-cycle model implies a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Observational analysis of administrative data from 100+ US retirement plans and a UK panel, plus a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete effect-size trajectory (12 vs 36 months) for exactly the persistence question the brief asks, and shows distributional (inequality-reducing) benefits can persist even as average gains shrink.
limitations: Employer/government-mandated retirement plans, not a consumer app
small, liquid round-up sums differ substantially from retirement accounts
relevance_reason: Directly quantifies attenuation of default effects between 12 and 36 months, the exact persistence question the brief poses, despite the employer-mediated setting.

key_finding: Across experiments including a 4,207-person five-country European study, default nudges produce medium-to-large effects on investment risk-taking, but also lower ratings of the wealth manager's advice — especially when the targeted default is refused — mediated by perceived honesty.
methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative multi-country European experiment on default framing in investment advice.
why_it_matters: Directly addresses the EU reputational-risk question in the brief: a default that shapes behavior can simultaneously damage users' trust in the institution, especially when rejected — a caution for how the round-up default and its exit flow should be framed.
limitations: Wealth-management investment context rather than a round-up savings pot
no persistence data beyond the experimental session
relevance_reason: European consumer-finance evidence on when a default reads as manipulative rather than helpful, exactly the dark-pattern risk the brief flags.

key_finding: At three large firms, automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate and fund, and half remained at the default rate/fund after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a pre-set default level strongly anchors the level people end up at for years, directly bearing on whether a pre-selected round-up multiplier will anchor most users below a higher tier.
limitations: Employer-sponsored 401(k), not a consumer app
predates the fintech/liquidity/regulatory context the brief says has changed
relevance_reason: The classic evidence for level-anchoring on pre-set defaults, the exact mechanism the brief worries about for the round-up multiplier choice.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost, and adding a lower preset menu option captures 69% of the achievable welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on transaction data plus an independent stated-preference survey, with counterfactual menu-design simulations.
why_it_matters: The friction-decomposition method and the counterfactual of adding a lower preset menu tier transfer directly to designing the round-up multiplier menu: it shows how a lower tier can recover most of the welfare loss from anchoring without abandoning presets.
limitations: Tipping decisions at point-of-sale, not a savings product
single-city taxi population, not banking-app users
relevance_reason: Explicit method transfer: its decomposition of default adherence into deviation-cost and opt-out-cost frictions, and its counterfactual of adding a lower menu option, is a directly applicable technique for designing the round-up multiplier menu.

key_finding: In a UK opt-in payroll short-term savings program, take-up was extremely low (at most 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account), but among adopters 96% still held a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
methodology: Field study of the introduction of an opt-in short-term, liquid, payroll-deduction savings account at five UK firms.
why_it_matters: Provides a rare data point on a liquid, withdrawable short-term savings product structurally close to a round-up pot: opt-in alone yields negligible reach but very durable engagement among adopters, sharpening the reach-versus-quality trade-off central to the entry decision.
limitations: Employer payroll-deduction channel, not a self-service consumer app
no comparison arm with opt-out or active choice
relevance_reason: The closest available product-structure analog (liquid, short-term, withdrawable savings) to the round-up pot, showing opt-in's take-up versus retention trade-off directly.

key_finding: Develops a general theoretical characterization of optimal default options, showing that when designer and choosers agree on an activity's value, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with further results for disagreement and externalities.
methodology: Theoretical mechanism-design model with asymptotic analysis validated by numerical simulations, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a normative framework for when defaulting people in is actually optimal versus when it is not, including the case where the firm and user disagree about the product's value — relevant to whether an opt-out design is justified or paternalistic.
limitations: Fully abstract theoretical model with no empirical application
no consumer-financial or savings context specified
relevance_reason: A domain-general normative model of optimal default design, useful for reasoning about when an opt-out default is justified versus manipulative, a live question in the brief.

key_finding: Maps EU dark-pattern law onto a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations, framing pre-selected defaults and similar choice-architecture practices as regulable when they undermine informed consumer decision-making.
methodology: Doctrinal/normative legal analysis of EU consumer-protection law; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly bears on the entry-design decision: it tells us where the line sits between a helpful opt-out default and a regulable dark pattern under EU law, which is the reputational and legal risk the brief flags for opt-out enrolment.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not empirical behavioural evidence
no financial-product-specific case studies or effect sizes
EU law framework, not a test of any particular default design
relevance_reason: Gives the EU-specific manipulation/dark-pattern framework the brief explicitly asks for when weighing opt-out against active choice.

key_finding: With a very high 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees still had not opted out after 12 months (vs. ~50% opt-out under lower defaults elsewhere), and many stayed anchored at 12% even though it was a suboptimal, unmatched contribution rate, especially lower-income employees.
methodology: Administrative panel data from one employer's retirement plan with a 12% default; compared against a literature review of lower-default opt-out rates.
why_it_matters: Strong quantitative evidence that a pre-set default anchors people at a level many would not have chosen and that this anchoring effect is stronger for lower-income (less sophisticated) users — directly relevant to how we choose the pre-selected multiplier and to the brief's who's-helped/who's-hurt question.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer self-directed app
no EU regulatory context
single-employer, 12-month horizon only
relevance_reason: Quantifies default anchoring and shows distributional harm to less-sophisticated savers, both core sub-questions of the brief.

key_finding: Using 41M observations, ~85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to active-choice subsidies but strongly moved by automatic (default) contributions, while the 15% of 'active savers' who respond to subsidies mostly just shift assets across accounts with $1 of subsidy raising total saving by only ~1 cent.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data (Danish population registers), natural policy variation in subsidies vs. automatic employer contributions.
why_it_matters: The clearest large-scale evidence on who is actually helped by defaults vs. active-choice mechanisms, and on the size of the gap — sets the effect-size ceiling and the distributional lens the brief asks us to apply, even though the setting is retirement rather than liquid savings.
limitations: employer/government-mediated retirement accounts, not a self-directed consumer app
Danish institutional context, not EU fintech regulatory setting
does not address active-choice-at-onboarding designs directly
relevance_reason: Foundational large-N evidence on default vs. active-choice effectiveness and on heterogeneous 'active' vs 'passive' saver types, informing the distributional criterion.

key_finding: Introduces and field-tests 'enhanced active choice' — active choice that highlights the losses of the non-preferred option — as an alternative to automatic enrollment when a straight default is infeasible or ethically fraught, explicitly proposed as a complement to automatic enrollment in savings contexts.
methodology: Review of prior active-choice literature plus a series of studies including two field experiments; abstract-only for effect sizes.
why_it_matters: This is the direct evidence base for the third onboarding option the brief is weighing — whether active choice captures most of the enrolment benefit without the opt-out disengagement cost — and it offers a concrete design variant (loss-framed active choice) the team could implement instead of a plain forced choice.
limitations: primary experiments are in medication-adherence, not financial, settings
abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes for the savings analogy
does not report persistence/withdrawal outcomes
relevance_reason: Directly addresses active choice vs. defaults and proposes a specific enhanced-active-choice mechanism the brief's onboarding decision could adopt.

key_finding: Synthesizes household-finance behavioural regularities and reviews interventions — education, defaults, product design, choice architecture — that firms and governments use to shape financial decisions, without a single new effect-size estimate.
methodology: Narrative review chapter (abstract-only, no systematic-review protocol stated).
why_it_matters: Gives the broad landscape of choice-architecture interventions in consumer (not just employer-plan) financial behaviour, useful context for weighing product-design levers like preset multipliers against blank fields, but not a source of a decision-specific number.
limitations: review chapter, not a primary study with effect sizes for our decisions
covers many domains beyond savings defaults
not EU-specific or app-specific
relevance_reason: Broad review of choice architecture in consumer finance that satisfies the brief's request for a synthesis piece, though it lacks decision-specific numbers.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment raised participation above 85% at three firms, but ~80% of participants initially accepted the low default savings rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half were still at the default rate and fund after three years, roughly offsetting the participation gain in aggregate wealth accumulation.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large firms with automatic 401(k) enrollment.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that defaults raise nominal enrolment but strongly anchor the contribution level and persist for years — exactly the anchoring-versus-vanity-enrolment tension the brief wants tested, giving the benchmark persistence figures (half still at default after 3 years).
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, pre-dates modern fintech/app context
no EU regulatory framing
locked, illiquid savings vehicle unlike round-up sums
relevance_reason: The foundational study on default persistence and anchoring that the newer, more relevant papers in this set are responding to.

key_finding: Randomizing default enrollment into a salary-linked savings account raised participation by 40 percentage points (equivalent to a 50% match), an effect the authors attribute mainly to present bias and the cognitive cost of thinking through savings scenarios, with defaults also making people more likely to actively choose to save afterward.
methodology: Randomized field experiment among salaried employees in Afghanistan, with follow-up interventions to isolate mechanisms.
why_it_matters: Offers a rare quantified, mechanism-level estimate of why defaults change savings behaviour and evidence that a default period can leave a lasting positive shift in active saving attitudes — relevant to whether an opt-out period could 'train' engagement rather than just producing passive enrolment.
limitations: salary-linked account in a developing-country context, not an EU consumer banking app
employer-facilitated payroll deduction rather than self-directed fintech enrolment
persistence measured via attitudes, not 6-12 month withdrawal/engagement data
relevance_reason: Provides a quantified default effect size and a mechanistic explanation for why defaults work, useful evidence for the persistence and engagement questions even though the setting differs.
